item.title: Zcash is Not Hard Money
item.author: arthur.sabintsev@gmail.com (Arthur Sabintsev)
item.description: Naval called ZEC insurance against Bitcoin. It does not pay out if Bitcoin fails, and the shielded supply is harder to audit than Bitcoin's.
item.content:encoded:
Naval called ZEC insurance against Bitcoin. It does not pay out if Bitcoin fails, and the shielded supply is harder to audit than Bitcoin's.

Naval got it wrong

When Naval Ravikant called Zcash "insurance against Bitcoin," the line worked because it made privacy sound like risk management.

But insurance pays when the thing you insured against fails.

ZEC, Zcash's token, does not pay if Bitcoin fails. If Bitcoin fails, the monetary network that makes ZEC interesting shrinks with it. ZEC is only mildly interesting if Bitcoin works so well that its transparent ledger becomes a liability.

Even then, surveillance only creates the opening. It does not prove ZEC is the asset that captures it.

Two risks

Bitcoin is a response to one kind of state risk: monetary discretion. Debasement, bailouts, capital controls, confiscatory policy, the slow political capture of money.

Bitcoin does not stop a government from printing money. It gives people an asset outside that issuance regime.

Zcash is aimed at a different risk: financial surveillance.

If Bitcoin becomes real settlement infrastructure, the chain becomes a searchable map of economic relationships. Exchanges label it. Analytics firms package it. Creditors, competitors, lawyers, and governments can query it.

Zcash's pitch is that people will pay to get off that graph. That can be useful, but it does not make ZEC Bitcoin.

Privacy

The obvious Bitcoiner objection is simple: privacy is a feature, not a separate monetary asset.

Use better wallets. CoinJoin, PayJoin, and Silent Payments improve the public map of who paid whom. Lightning moves everyday payments off the public ledger, although it leaks different metadata and is not Monero-style privacy. Fedimint adds private digital cash held by a small group you have to trust. None of this is perfect, but that is the Bitcoiner point: privacy can keep moving into Bitcoin without making ZEC the asset that captures it.

If Bitcoin leaks too much metadata, the Bitcoiner fix is to make Bitcoin usage less leaky.

ZEC has to prove more than privacy matters. It has to prove the privacy value belongs in a separate money.

Monero

Monero is the cleaner privacy-coin comparison because it does not pretend to be Bitcoin with a privacy upgrade.

Monero chose privacy-first cash. Its transactions are private by default. It also has no fixed maximum supply. Under the current consensus rules, Monero's tail emission stays at 0.6 XMR, Monero's token, per block indefinitely, so miners keep getting paid after the main emission.

Monero's messaging is coherent: privacy-first money, predictable ongoing issuance.

Zcash wants the Bitcoin scarcity story and the privacy story at the same time. The privacy system is exactly what makes the scarcity claim harder to audit in the Bitcoin sense.

Auditability

Bitcoin is not private. Its stronger claim is that the money is publicly verifiable. Run a node and the supply either adds up or it doesn't. You are not asking a foundation, a lab, or a cryptographer to certify the monetary base.

Zcash is different. It has transparent addresses and shielded addresses. The shielded side hides addresses and amounts while still letting nodes check that a transaction follows the rules without seeing who paid whom or how much.

The public chain can count value moving into and out of shielded pools through turnstiles. It cannot inspect every private note inside the pool the way a Bitcoin node can inspect each unspent coin in the open.

A ZEC buyer is not getting Bitcoin's audit model with privacy bolted on for free. They are buying a system where private payments depend on the proofs staying sound, on that count of value in and out, on audits, upgrades, and the judgment of the people maintaining the shielded pool.

Orchard

Orchard, Zcash's current shielded-pool system, made the hard-money claim harder to defend. Shielded Labs said a local exploit could create counterfeit ZEC inside the shielded pool. Zcash Foundation said there was no evidence it happened on the live network, and turnstiles showed total supply had not leaked past the pool boundary.

This is not the first time Zcash has had to repair confidence in a shielded pool, which is part of the problem in viewing ZEC as hard money. If the privacy layer needs periodic expert maintenance to defend the monetary claim, the supply claim depends on that maintenance.

ZEC is Unnecessary

Bitcoin's strongest pitch is self-custodied savings with a supply users can verify for themselves.

Zcash's strongest pitch is that your payments should not be easy for strangers to look up.

ZEC can be useful if Bitcoin wins and becomes watched. But if ZEC needs Bitcoin to create the demand, and then needs expert coordination when its private audit layer breaks, it is not insurance against Bitcoin. It is a surveillance hedge trying to borrow Bitcoin's money story, even though Monero already shows that privacy can be valuable without pretending to be Bitcoin. That is the part I don't buy.

item.title: Tokens Never Die
item.author: arthur.sabintsev@gmail.com (Arthur Sabintsev)
item.description: When a project stops shipping, the token keeps trading. Volume bots, momentum bots, MEV, and pump groups are the aftermarket.
item.content:encoded:
When a project stops shipping, the token keeps trading. Volume bots, momentum bots, MEV, and pump groups are the aftermarket.

When a public company runs out of money there's a legal off-ramp. The court closes the cap table, the list of who owns the company. Shares are marked to zero on a specific date.

Token contracts have none of that. They keep executing transfers on every chain until the validators that secure that chain go offline.

The token is its own product, during the project's life and after. It tends to have no bearing on the work. The price tracks attention, narrative, and bots, not output.

So when a project stops shipping, the token doesn't die. It gets an afterlife, and the afterlife has its own economy.

The Food Chain

Four algorithmic layers stack on every dead token with a stranded liquidity pool, the LP that nobody pulled when the project quit, still holding the token against ETH (ether), SOL (Solana), USDC (a dollar stablecoin), or whatever it was paired with.

Volume bots. Paid services that manufacture trades between rotating wallets. Chainalysis traced one operator, Volume.li, to $257.5 million in cumulative fake volume. Packages are priced by output: tiers run from $50 of manufactured volume in 24 hours up to $100,000 in 24 hours. As of Chainalysis's 2025 reporting, the top tier cost about 0.2 ETH. The whole category exists to push pairs onto DEXScreener, DEXTools, Photon, and pump.fun trending feeds, because aggregator algorithms reward volume.

Momentum bots. Algorithmic traders watching the trending feeds and piling into anything that spikes. No thesis on the project.

MEV and sandwich bots. MEV is the cut from ordering someone else's trade. On illiquid pairs a small trade moves the price, so the buy just before that trade and the sell just after both pay. Sandwich extraction on Ethereum cooled from roughly $10 million a month in late 2024 to $2.5 million by October 2025, but the bots never leave. Solana's Jito ecosystem runs the same playbook with different plumbing. Sandwich bots have extracted between $370 and $500 million from Solana traders over a 16-month window, and even after Jito, Marinade, and the Solana Foundation blacklisted 50+ malicious validators in 2025, October still saw roughly 18,000 SOL pulled from 200,000 victims.

Pump groups. They understand the food chain better than the average founder ever did. Find a zombie with a stranded LP. Accumulate quietly while attention is elsewhere. Fire a coordinated buy at a known block or slot. The volume spike registers on DEXScreener and pump.fun trending. The momentum bots watching those feeds pile in. The MEV bots trade immediately after every new trade. The pump group sells into that climbing bot stack. Retail isn't there anymore.

Chainalysis counted 2.06 million tokens launched in 2024. Only 1.7% had meaningful trading inside thirty days. Layer in launches on pump.fun (the Solana site for minting a new token), every token on a Cosmos chain built for one app, every memecoin on a layer-2 chain (a chain that settles onto a larger one), and the dead population is bigger than any single chain's data captures. The 98.3% don't go to zero. They go quiet for a while, and then they're raised from the dead.

item.title: Your Token Was An Equity Grant All Along
item.author: arthur.sabintsev@gmail.com (Arthur Sabintsev)
item.description: Customers want the work priced in dollars. Operators still hold the token for the upside.
item.content:encoded:
Customers want the work priced in dollars. Operators still hold the token for the upside.

Most customers don't want your token. They want a GPU hour, an RPC call from a wallet to a node, a map mile, storage, vehicle data, wireless coverage, and so on. Price that in dollars and the buyer can budget. Price it in the network's own token and the buyer becomes an unwitting community member inheriting your baggage: treasury policy, tax treatment, and a view on your price chart.

DePIN (decentralized physical infrastructure, the networks that pay people to run hardware) made that trade because the industry was scared to say the obvious. Between 2018 and 2022, a token that looked like ownership also looked like the thing the SEC's digital-asset framework called an investment contract. So networks gave tokens jobs: gas, the fee for a transaction, plus access, settlement, security, and governance.

Anything except a cap table (the list of who owns the company), which is funny, because the token was behaving like equity all along, and that equity-like upside landed on the network operators.

Payroll Is Not Capital

Operators don't run on upside. They run on operating costs: power, bandwidth, GPUs, rent, labor, and taxes. Those are dollar liabilities. Pay them in a token that can lose 90% from peak in eighteen months, as HNT, Helium's token, did, and a hardware business unwittingly gets a trading desk attached.

The unemotional, disciplined operators sell immediately on receipt. Hedging isn't really on the menu, because most DePIN tokens don't have perpetual futures or options deep enough to short. The holders ride the price down and leave. Capacity goes first, then quality, then demand.

When operators are paid in the token, their profit and loss and the token chart become the same chart.

The Networks That Recovered

The networks that recovered split the two assets: the token for ownership, and for the work a dollar stablecoin or tokens the recipient cannot sell yet.

Render prices jobs in ordinary currency and burns RENDER, its token, on settlement.

Filecoin Onchain Cloud streams USDFC, a dollar-pegged Filecoin stablecoin, through Filecoin Pay directly to storage providers.

DIMO sells vehicle data through credits. Hivemapper sells map credits and pays contributors in HONEY, its token.

IO.net takes USDC, a dollar stablecoin, from customers and pays suppliers in IO, its token.

Akash named the trade-off in writing when they shipped Burn-Mint Equilibrium: stable payments help adoption but can weaken native-token demand, while native-token payments keep token demand alive but scare buyers and squeeze providers. They picked stable pricing with native-token settlement and moved on.

Pocket Network, which I helped build, was early to a different primitive: apps lock up POKT, Pocket's token, to reserve request capacity instead of paying per call. That keeps the customer (demand) side off the token-price treadmill and supplies buy-pressure, but node runners (supply-side) still earn POKT and still face the same selling pressure as every other DePIN operator. PIP-41, a Pocket proposal, closes part of that gap with a deflationary mint: every request served burns more POKT than it mints, so usage tightens supply instead of inflating it. Operators still earn POKT, but the POKT they hold appreciates with the network's success rather than getting diluted by it.

Helium prices data in USD-pegged Data Credits, minted by burning HNT. Messari's 2025 DePIN report shows what that fix is producing in practice: Helium's revenue on the chain grew 8x in 2025 while HNT fell 77%. The token is decoupling from operational performance, which is what equity does. Operators still earned HNT and still ate the drawdown, so the supply side remains the harder fix, but the token's behavior in the data is already telling you what the token actually is. Split from the work, the token starts behaving like a standalone financial product priced on what the network might be worth in five years, not what it earned this quarter.

The Token Is The Cap Table

Different designs, same admission: work needs insulation from token volatility, and the token should do the one job nobody else can, which is to represent ownership.

Strip away the story that the token has to pay for the work, and a DePIN token looks less like money and more like an employee stock option. Operators show up before revenue is real. They buy hardware, sign leases, keep machines online, and take reputational risk on a network most customers haven't heard of yet. Cash pays for the month, and the token is the upside if the network matters five years later. That's a barbell payoff, and it's the same shape as every Series A engineer's comp package: small monthly draw, large terminal upside, conditional on the product actually mattering.

Look at the analogies. Emissions are the option pool. Burns are buybacks. Staking is the vesting cliff. Slashing is clawback. AKT, Akash's token, is its incentive pool. Collateral posted in FIL, Filecoin's token, is Filecoin's clawback. POKT burns are explicitly deflationary, funded by app demand. None of that requires the same token to denominate the work itself.

This is the useful DePIN invention, and the industry still under-sells it. A public company can't hand meaningful equity to an individual hardware operator without lawyers, transfer agents, jurisdiction checks, tax paperwork, and a lot of "we'll get back to you." That's the friction for a Frankfurt-based Render miner or a Singapore-based Akash provider. For a Hivemapper driver in São Paulo or a Helium hotspot host in rural Kansas, the legal scaffolding barely exists at all. A tokenized network can grant upside in a block. DePIN accidentally built what functions like a global ESOP, an employee stock ownership plan, for operators public markets can't structurally reach.

The token functions as a claim on whatever the network becomes. The Hivemapper driver who shot map data in 2023 and the Helium hotspot host who built coverage in 2021 each hold a slice of however much those networks are worth in 2030.

item.title: The Resilience Premium
item.author: arthur.sabintsev@gmail.com (Arthur Sabintsev)
item.description: A second vendor fails as a backup when it goes down for the same reason as the first.
item.content:encoded:
A second vendor fails as a backup when it goes down for the same reason as the first.

I've been wanting to write this since early 2024.

Most software doesn't need decentralization. Gmail works. S3 works. Stripe works. Centralized providers win the happy path because the happy path rewards speed, polish, support, and procurement simplicity.

Redundancy Is Not Resilience

Having a second vendor is the easy part. The test is whether your backup fails for a different reason than your primary.

Most redundancy doesn't pass that test. AWS, Azure, GCP, Cloudflare, major RPC vendors (the companies a wallet calls for chain data), and AI providers still share internet routing, DNS, identity systems, software supply chains, political compliance regimes, and capital-market incentives. Three vendors that fail for the same reason are functionally one.

When Multi-Vendor Still Goes Dark

Cloudflare's June 2025 outage is the clean example. Workers KV failed for 2 hours and 28 minutes after an underlying third-party cloud dependency went down. Roughly 90% of requests failed, and the same dependency broke several other Cloudflare products.

The Tornado Cash sanctions showed a different kind of correlation. After OFAC (the U.S. Treasury's sanctions office) sanctioned Tornado Cash (a mixer that hides the payment trail) in August 2022, Alchemy and Infura blocked RPC access.

Unless you were running your own node, or routing through your own gateway on a decentralized network, you couldn't reach the contract.

The two biggest vendors were affected by one compliance regime, and all users were locked out of the contract.

What Blockchains Actually Add

Nobody pays the premium because they believe in decentralization. They pay it so their backup doesn't go down on the same day their primary does.

A better name for the premium is resilience capacity: a backup that fails for reasons unrelated to your primary.

Blockchains made this practical. Tokens didn't make networks faster or fix bad products. They let you pay and coordinate independent operators across jurisdictions and balance sheets.

The Market Is Already Pricing It

Developer tooling is already multi-provider.

  • viem ships fallback transports
  • ethers ships a FallbackProvider
  • MetaMask's DIN, its Decentralized Infrastructure Network, routes through more than 50 independent providers.

Regulators are pricing the same risk. EU DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, requires financial entities to manage how dependent they are on any single tech provider and to plan for multi-vendor alternatives.

Insurers are writing policies on it. Parametrix and Riskwolf sell cloud-outage coverage that pays when a measured outage crosses a set trigger.

Who Buys Resilience Capacity?

The buyer is a wallet that can't go dark on any given Sunday, an exchange that can't lose read/write access when one provider changes policy, or an AI company that doesn't want one model vendor as a permanent chokepoint.

Axe Compute (NASDAQ: AGPU) closed a $260M multi-year deal sourcing 2,304 GPUs through Aethir's decentralized network, wrapped in enterprise SLAs (the contracts for uptime and support). I believe that is the buyer: a public company that needs decentralized supply for the resilience and a US-listed counterparty for the contract.

The Better Pitch

Two pitches the industry should retire:

  • "We're faster than the centralized provider." Most of the time, you won't be.
  • "Decentralization is always better." It isn't.

Use the centralized provider on a normal day. Pay for a backup that fails for a different reason.
